source.title: Generalizable Adversarial Training via Spectral Normalization
source.authors: F. Farnia; Jesse M. Zhang; David Tse

record.tranche_reason: Tests random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under adversarial training, extending the memorization/generalization question to adversarial training and spectral normalization.
record.gate_note: Figure 4 reports training curves for random and true labels; exact values are not stated, and it does not report held-out accuracy on random labels. Table 1 reports natural-label train and test accuracy before and after spectral normalization. Results cited from other studies are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The study extends V1's random-label fitting comparison to adversarial training. Its own results also bear on V3 through convolutional-versus-MLP accuracy comparisons and on V6 through a dropout control.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors conclude that spectral normalization generally improves adversarial test performance and generalization across their tested settings. Their AlexNet/CIFAR-10 experiments also show harder fitting of random and true labels, while appropriately selected normalization retains or improves true-label held-out performance. They do not establish universal improvement.
record.recipe_differences: Uses adversarial training with FGM, PGM, or WRM and adds spectral normalization; the claim version concerns standard training on natural data. The study does not report held-out random-label accuracy.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects vary by dataset, architecture, and adversarial-training scheme; the authors report improvement in almost all experiments, with some cases where spectral normalization lowers test accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Spectral normalization generally improves adversarial held-out accuracy and makes random and true labels harder to fit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-validated spectral normalization can improve adversarial generalization while restricting fitting capacity. Its reduced random-label fitting is outside V1's condition without explicit regularization.

fits_no_version.finding: Spectral-norm capacity terms and normalized margins yield tighter theoretical generalization bounds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Spectral-norm and margin-based capacity control can tighten adversarial generalization bounds; this does not measure the magnitude-aware sharpness ranking named in V7.

record.problems: Random-label results are shown only as training curves, without numeric values or held-out random-label accuracy. Table 1 reports test accuracy but does not report uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: No rows. Figure 4's plotted random-label and true-label training curves lack separable numeric values; the table reports natural-label results but cannot establish the held-out random-label comparison required by V1.

untested.parts: Held-out accuracy on random labels is not reported. Random-label fitting is examined for AlexNet on CIFAR-10, not all architectures and datasets named in V1.
No width sweep or test-error comparison beyond interpolation.
No isolation of local connectivity, learned sparse connections, or initialization from a trained convolutional network.
No dropout-rate sweep, very-small-dataset comparison, or joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
No empirical ranking of generalization gaps by magnitude-aware sharpness or comparison against competing measures.
No removal of memorized training examples.

missing.what: Extract the CIFAR-10 convolutional-versus-MLP comparisons as evidence for V3. The record declares Table 1 omitted for its inability to establish all of V1, but overlooks its independent architectural comparison: ERM test accuracies are 0.79/0.85/0.80 for AlexNet/Inception/ResNet and 0.49/0.51 for one-/two-hidden-layer MLPs.

Extract the dropout control: no regularization gives train/validation accuracy 1.00/0.48; dropout rate 0.8 gives 0.99/0.52. Preserve validation as the held-out split and use Figure 11's own baseline rather than Table 1's test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: The record contains no rows, so verdicts use the supplied text and have empty row_ids. V1's Figure 4 and Table 1 omissions are already declared in rows_left_out. No precise random-label endpoint can be recovered from the supplied figure text. The study is not an original source for these versions. Spectral normalization's suppression of memorization does not challenge V1 because it adds explicit regularization.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests random-label fitting and natural-label generalization in adversarial training, not the stated standard-training recipes. It does not report held-out accuracy on random labels, so the random-label chance comparison is untested.

relationships.condition: AlexNet on CIFAR-10 without spectral normalization, under ERM and adversarial training
relationships.reason: Based on text rather than extracted rows: Section 5.2 reports random-label fitting with only slight delays under adversarial training; Table 1 gives natural-label test accuracies of 0.79 for ERM and 0.50–0.61 for the corresponding FGM/PGM ℓ2 and WRM settings, above 0.10 chance. The random-label held-out component remains untested.
relationships.display_finding: The reported random-label fitting alongside natural-label test generalization remains unverified for the paired training settings.
